The Northern red-sided opossum, Monodelphis brevicaudata, exhibits a notably rapid pace of development during its early life stages. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the gestation period has been documented to last 12.5 days [tg = 12.5 days], a remarkably short interval that aligns with the general pattern of accelerated embryonic development seen in small-bodied didelphid marsupials. Shortly after completing this brief uterine phase, the altricial newborn pups emerge weighing a mere 0.1 grams [Wwb = 0.1 grams], a value that is quite typical for the family Didelphidae and underscores the extreme altriciality of neonatal opossums. These tiny offspring are heavily dependent on maternal care, immediately attaching to the teats within the female's pouch, where they will continue their development in a protected environment.

Following parturition, the suckling juveniles experience a prolonged period of dependency within the maternal pouch and nest. Field records indicate that weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the onset of nutritional independence, occurs at approximately 68 days after birth [tx = approximately 68 days after birth] when the animals are reared at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This relatively extended nursing phase is critical for the pups, allowing them to grow substantially and develop the necessary motor skills for independent foraging. The dietary transition from milk to solid food, primarily consisting of insects and small invertebrates found in the leaf litter, marks a significant physiological milestone. The timing of this event likely influences subsequent growth trajectories and the overall pace of life history events in this species. Observations suggest that a stable thermal environment is crucial for ensuring a successful weaning process and high offspring survival rates.

As the young opossums continue to mature, they navigate a defined timeline toward reproductive capability. Data derived from studies on the closely related species Marmosa robinsoni suggest that individuals of Monodelphis brevicaudata reach puberty at approximately 180 days after birth [tp = approximately 180 days after birth] when maintained under a consistent thermal environment of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This extended period from weaning to the onset of gonadal activity likely reflects the time required for the weaned juvenile to accumulate sufficient body reserves and achieve the necessary skeletal and physiological maturity. During this juvenile phase, individuals undergo substantial growth, transitioning from their minimal birth mass to the dimensions characteristic of a breeding adult. The onset of puberty is a pivotal event, marking the point at which an individual transitions into a potentially reproductively active member of the population capable of contributing to the next generation.

The reproductive output of adult females is a key component of the species' life history strategy. Analysis of litters reveals that a single reproductive event typically consists of seven pups per litter [N_R_i = seven pups per litter]. Over the course of a year, a female may produce between one and two litters [F_R_i = Over the course of a year, a female may produce between one and two litters], a pattern that is typical for small marsupials with a relatively fast life history. This annual reproductive output is closely tied to resource availability and is often maximized under favorable environmental conditions. Upon reaching full maturity, adult females of this species attain a typical ultimate body mass of 95 grams [Wwi = 95 grams], though a range of 67 to 95 grams is commonly observed in wild populations. This mass represents a tremendous increase from the 0.1 gram birth weight and supports the energetic demands of gestation and lactation found in breeding females.

The metabolism and overall lifespan of Monodelphis brevicaudata further define its ecological niche. Basal metabolic rate measurements taken from individuals at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] indicate a maximum consumption of 75.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 75.50 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This rate of oxygen consumption reflects the high energetic costs associated with maintaining a stable body temperature and supporting the metabolic demands of a small, active endotherm. Comparative data from Marmosa robinsoni allow researchers to estimate the maximum lifespan for this species. Under ideal captive conditions, it is believed that an individual could live for approximately 3.9 years [am = approximately 3.9 years] when maintained at a stable temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This relatively short maximum longevity, combined with its rapid early development, places this opossum firmly on the fast end of the mammalian life-history continuum.
